thread.title: State Of The Economy 16: The Fed Likely Just Started The Next Stock Market Rally

author: Dividend Sensei
title: State Of The Economy 16: The Fed Likely Just Started The Next Stock Market Rally
text:
(Source: imgflip )
Note that due to reader requests, I've decided to break up my weekly portfolio updates into three parts: commentary, economic update, portfolio summary/stats/watch lists. This is to avoid excessively long articles and maximize the utility to my readers.
This week's commentary/listicle highlights the 3 best high-yield, recession-proof dividend aristocrats you can buy today .
Introduction Note that I offer these weekly economic updates purely because I believe that investors should always take a holistic "big picture view" of the world. That means knowing the state of the economy and what the short- and medium-term recession risks likely are. However, as I'll explain later in this article (recession risk section), macroeconomic analysis has historically proven to be a terrible tool for stock market timing ( SPY ) ( DIA ) ( QQQ ). Which is why I only offer these analyses so that readers will likely be able to see a recession coming about a year or so away.
That will hopefully allow you the time to prepare yourself emotionally and financially for the downturn. It will also hopefully allow you to adjust your portfolio's capital allocation to a more defensive stance, such as with defensive sectors, or potentially greater allocation to bonds (for lower risk-tolerant investors).
The Fed Delivers The Christmas Gift Wall Street Was Hoping For... For months investors have worried that the Fed would hike us into a recession and a bear market. That's because the Fed's latest dot plot, or long-term Fed Fund Rate guidance, showed either five, or even six more hikes coming through the end of 2020.
(Source: FOMC)
What's worse on October 3rd, Fed Chairman Powell helped to trigger the market panic that turned into the second correction of 2018 when he said that “ we’re a long way from neutral at this point. ” By neutral he meant the estimated neutral Fed Fund Rate that neither accelerates nor reduces the economy's growth rate. Currently, Fed members estimate that rate could be anywhere from 2.5% to 3.5%, with 3% being the consensus estimate.
But on Wednesday, November 28th, Powell set the market on fire (2.3% gain) by walking back his earlier hawkish remark. Specifically, he said that interest rates “remain just below the broad range of estimates of the level that would be neutral for the economy.” That might not sound that important but for the Fed, whose members know their every word is parsed to death by market analysts, it's a huge improvement.
What's more, the Fed's Vice Chairman Richard Clarida also told reporters last week that the University of Michigan consumer inflation expectations for the next five to 10 years are “within - but I believe at the lower end of - the range consistent with price stability.” What this bit of Fed-speak means is that the Fed is now starting to worry about inflation not getting too high, but too low.
(Source: Burea of Economic Analysis )
The Fed's official goal is to keep the Personal Consumption Expenditure index, excluding food and fuel (naturally volatile) at 2.0% over time. The BEA's latest estimate of core inflation is now showing the Fed's official inflation gauge not just not rising above 2.0% but actually falling over the last three months.
The Fed is concerned that if inflation gets too low, then we might fall into deflation or an overall decline in consumer prices. The theoretical reason this could be bad is that if prices are falling over time, consumers might think "why buy stuff today if it will be cheaper in the future". Since 65% to 70% of the US economy is driven by consumer spending, deflation could theoretically (in the Fed's view) become a self-fulfilling prophecy in which falling prices lead to consumer spending declining, triggering a recession and thus further price declines.
In reality, that is a silly fear given that consumers will not put off staple good purchases (like gas and food) because they think they will be cheaper tomorrow. More likely the REAL reason that deflation is feared is that a highly indebted society (and government) counts on moderate inflation to help decrease the effective amount of loans that need to be paid back.
But in either case, the Fed doesn't want inflation below 2% over the long term, and right now the bond market is signaling that's what's coming down the pike.
That's because the bond market's 10-year inflation expectations (of the Consumer Price Index) have recently dived 0.2% since peaking October 8th. CPE is generally slightly above the PCE inflation metric which means that the bond market is now predicting that core inflation will run below the Fed's target over the next decade.
Which brings us to the even more important interest rate news from last week. That would be the November Fed minutes release. These showed that the Fed is bent on at least one more hike in December. “Almost all participants expressed the view that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate was likely to be warranted fairly soon."
But what cheered investors was that the minutes showed the Fed is now officially ending its previous gradual (every quarter) hiking plan and will take a flexible approach.
“Many participants indicated that it might be appropriate at some upcoming meetings to begin to transition to statement language that placed greater emphasis on the evaluation of incoming data in assessing the economic and policy outlook ... Such a change would help to convey the committee’s flexible approach. ” - Fed November minutes (emphasis added)
The minutes also signaled a change in the Fed's official policy statement “particularly the language referring to the committee’s expectations for further gradual increases.”
Further gradual increases is Fed-speak for "we'll hike every 3 months until something forces us to stop". What might that something be?
“Several participants were concerned that the high level of debt in the non-financial business sector , and especially the high level of leveraged loans , made the economy more vulnerable to a sharp pullback in credit availability.” - Fed November minutes (emphasis added)
What does all this technocratic jargon really mean for investors and the future of short-term interest rates? Well, here's what the bond futures market now expects from the Fed in the future.
Number of Rate Hikes Through The End Of 2019 Probability 1 More (December) 96.1% 2 More 70.7% 3 More
32.7% 4 More 9.2% 5 More 1.6% (Source: CME Group )
In early October, the bond market was forecasting the Fed would hike 3 more times and then stop.
Now the bond market expects just two more hikes and then the Fed Funds rate (and consumer borrowing rates with it) will have peaked this cycle. Similarly, short-term Treasury yields, which tend to track closely with the FFR (and which were pricing in three more hikes) are likely to also peak soon if they haven't already.
That basically means we're NOT likely to get the higher interest rates that the market feared would force valuation multiples lower and thus theoretically hurt stocks. But it's important to remember that the Fed's "gift" to Wall Street isn't necessarily a good thing.
...BUT That Also Comes With A Major Downside And The Balance Sheet Roll-Off Remains In Effect
The 2/10 yield curve, the most popular recession warning sign investors track, has been holding up relatively well during the correction (flight to safety lowering long-term yields). But now it's down to 0.21%, a sharp decline from its October 5th high (right after that hawkish Powell statement).
Now, of course, it's true that the 2/10 curve is still artificially suppressed (QE pushed it lower by 0.85% according to the Fed's own study). Even with the Fed's recent balance sheet roll off, the 2/10 curve is likely 0.7% depressed.
But that doesn't mean we can just use an "adjusted 2/10 yield curve" of 0.9% and rest easy that a recession is still many years away. That's because the 2/30 yield curve was not affected by Fed bond buying and that too has been falling due to the rapid decline in long-term inflation expectations (due to the weaker long-term growth outlook).
The 2/30 curve inversion has approximately an identical predictive power regarding recession timing (also predicts a recession about 17 months in advance). With the 2/30 curve, there's good news and bad news. The bad news is that the curve is down to 0.5%, which gives us a lot less safety cushion than the 0.9% we might estimate with an adjusted 2/10 curve. But the good news is the 2/30 curve has been roughly stable for the last two months, indicating the bond market does NOT expect a yield curve inversion is imminent.
Rather the bond market is merely expecting:
permanently slower growth of 2% to 2.5% (in line with "new normal" from 2010 to 2016); inflation below 2% for foreseeable future; and no 2/30 inversion in foreseeable future (possibly no recession until beyond 2021 at the earliest). But that doesn't necessarily mean we can call off the recession watch either.
(Source: Council On Foreign Relations )
According to Benn Steil, a senior fellow, and director of international economics at the Council on Foreign Relations, the Fed's balance sheet roll-off is set to create an effective FFR of about 4.75% by the end of 2019 (if we get just two more rate hikes).
Remember the Fed is now allowing $50 billion of bonds mature without reinvesting them (roll off). Thus far, the Fed has given no indication that the roll-off, which is sucking $300 billion out of the money supply each year, will be ending anytime soon.
Thus, even if the Fed ends its regular hiking plan after two more hikes (which would also help cool the economy all on its own), the roll-off might continue to slow growth beyond that, at least until the Fed ends that program. Again, I'm not trying to scare anyone, and don't expect the Fed to necessarily make a policy mistake that takes the economy into a recession. But my point is that investors will want to continue to monitor the macro fundamentals closely in 2019 and beyond because we're not out of the woods just yet.
Current Economic Growth Q3: 3.5% (second estimate) Q4: About 2.6% Full Year 2018: About 2.9% (IMF Estimate, best growth in 13 years) (Source: Atlanta Federal Reserve)
Every major GDP model uses slightly different combinations and weightings on leading indicators to estimate the current growth rate of the economy. Thus, the actual weekly figure is far less important than the trend of the estimate.
The Atlanta Fed's model is for once being conservative; the growth estimate is tracking the consensus expectation of 2.6% growth in Q4.
(Source: New York Federal Reserve)
The New York Fed's GDP model, which tends to err on the conservative side, is similarly estimating 2.5% growth for Q4. This is the first time in several quarters that both models have matched up so closely.
(Source: now-casting.com )
Nowcasting is currently estimating 3.6% GDP growth in Q4, which is not just much higher than the other estimates but also trending higher recently. This third estimate is currently an outlier compared to the Atlanta consensus and New York estimates. Thus, I consider it the upper end of possible economic growth this quarter. For my own forecast, I've gone with the consensus figure, which seems reasonable given the current economic data and headwinds we're facing.
Finally, periodically Capital Spectator compiles all seven nowcast GDP estimates, which show a median estimate of 2.7% growth, which I consider reasonable.
(Source: capitalspectator )
That would mean 2018 GDP Growth of:
Q1: 2.2% Q2: 4.2% Q3: 3.5% Q4: 2.6% Full Year: 2.9% (IMF Forecast) While the initial estimates of Q4 growth are disappointing, we're still on track for our best growth year since 2005. Sadly, it appears that we'll still miss achieving a full 3% growth year (2005 was the last time that happened).
If Q4 growth comes in at the 2.6% level that currently looks likely, that would signal that next year's 2.5% growth estimates are reasonable. 2% to 2.5% GDP growth is not a rate that will cause rising inflation that would cause the Fed to hike beyond the neutral rate (3 more times). So, while many might be disappointed if we return to weaker growth rates of the last few years, it would ultimately be beneficial in terms of extending the current economic expansion and keeping the bull market intact for another few years.
Recession Risk: Very Low The probability that we're in a recession right now: 0.24% The probability of a recession starting in the next three months: 1.2% The probability of a recession starting in the next nine months: 19% I use seven key meta-analyses to track the health of the economy. That includes those which have historically proven to be good predictors of recessions:
The 2/10 yield curve; The Base Line and Rate of Change or BaR economic graph; Jeff Miller's meta-analysis of leading economic indicators; The St. Louis Fed's smoothed-out recession risk indicator; and The New York, Atlanta Fed's and now-casting.com 's real-time GDP growth trackers.
(Source: Business Insider )
The yield curve has proven the single most accurate predictor of recessions over the past 80 years. Specifically, when the curve inverts or goes below 0 (because short-term rates rise above long-term rates), then a recession becomes highly likely. It usually begins within 12-18 months.

(Source: St. Louis Federal Reserve, Ben Carlson)
According to a March 2018 report from the San Francisco Fed, an inverted yield curve has " correctly signaled all nine recessions since 1955 and had only one false positive, in the mid-1960s, when an inversion was followed by an economic slowdown but not an official recession."
In other words, if the yield curve goes negative, there is probably a 90% chance of a recession starting within the next 17 months or so.
Unfortunately, investors hoping to use the yield curve to time market tops are out of luck. While a yield curve inversion is very accurate at predicting recessions with long lead times, its track record on predicting bear markets is far less impressive.
2/10 Yield Curve Inversion Vs. Bear Market Starts
(Source: Wealth Of Common Sense)
The lag time between market tops and yield curve inversions is all over the map, ranging from just 2 months in 2000 to nearly 2 years in 2005.
And if we go back to 1956 (using the 1/10 yield curve), we can also see that yield curve inversions are largely useless for timing bear market starts. In fact, on three occasions, the forward-looking market has actually peaked before the curve inverted. This means that the yield curve should not be used as a market timing mechanism but rather purely as a good recession risk indicator.
Current 2/10 Yield Curve: 0.21% (down from 0.24% last week) Since November 1st, the yield curve has fallen 9 basis points. But, typically, the 7/10 yield curve inverts first (by 6 to 28 days). It is currently 0.09%, nicely above a low of 0.04% a few months ago, indicating the short-term risk of a 2/10 yield curve inversion remains low. The 7/10 warning curve has remained strong and stable, as has the 2/30 curve. Most likely, we won't get an inversion in 2018, but Q1 2019 at the earliest and might not get a 2/30 inversion at all if the Fed only hikes two more times as the bond market now expects.
But it's important to remember that you shouldn't fear a flat yield curve as a sign of poor short- to medium-term stock performance.
During the strongest bond market in US history (tech boom), the yield curve was as low or even lower than it is now. Of course, that was also an epic bubble, but the point is that a flat, but positive yield curve is not a sign of poor returns ahead.
Average Monthly Stock Market Returns By 2/10 Yield Curve Slope (Since 1976)
(Source: Bloomberg )
In fact, over the past 42 years, the period when monthly stock returns were at their highest and volatility was at its lowest was when the yield curve was flat but positive. This means that we're likely in the sweet spot right now, and investors should avoid using fears of yield curve inversion as a reason for market timing.
That's because even after an inversion occurs, stocks tend to continue rising for quite some time and tend to generate strong returns before the next bear market begins.
Basically, the yield curve is a totally binary indicator.
positive = very low recession risk (carry on with long-term investing plans) negative = 90% chance recession is coming within 6 to 24 months (most likely 18 months) - consider getting more defensive The second economic indicator I watch is David Rice's (aka Economic PI) baseline and rate of change, or BaR economic analysis grid. This is another meta-analysis incorporating 19 leading indicators that track every aspect of the US economy. That includes the yield curve, though a different version of it. I consider it the best overall indicator of fundamental economic health (because it's so granular).
(Source: Economic PI )
The BaR grid has shown to be a reliable indicator, predicting the 1980, 1990, 2001, and 2007 recessions.
(Source: David Rice)
Currently, 16 out of 19 economic indicators are pointing to positive economic growth with just three to negative growth. This is among the strongest readings I've seen I've been doing economic updates (and one of the best readings in over two years).
(Source: David Rice)
Note that over the past 33 weeks, the number of leading indicators in the decline quadrant has ranged from three to 10. In any given week, one or two indicators might flip-flop between decelerating or accelerating growth. This is just statistical noise, and only long-term trends should be used as recession risk warning signs.
(Source: David Rice)
Both the three-month and 12-month trends remain highly positive and currently moving in the right direction (continued growth). Most important of all, the mean of coordinates or MOC continues to remain high, though it is now down from 35.3% two weeks ago. But that too doesn't necessarily indicate trouble because as you can see, the rolling 3-month MOC average has experienced periods of slowing growth (height above baseline) in the past without any recession occurring.
(Source: David Rice)
Next, there's Jeff Miller's excellent economic indicator snapshot, a rich source of numerous useful market/economic data. It also provides an actual percentage probability estimate for how likely a recession is to start in the next few months.
(Source: Jeff Miller )
What I'm looking at here is the quantitative estimates of short-term recession risks. In this case, the four-month recession risk is about 1.2%, while the probability of a recession starting within nine months is down from 24% to 19%. The short-term recession risk is highly volatile, ranging from 0.24% to 3.32% since I began tracking the economy over that past seven months. Thus, the more important thing to focus on isn't the absolute figure but the trends in both short-term and medium-term recession risks. Both have shown low risks, with the 9-month recession risk being highly stable at 24% all year, and now falling to just 19%. That's cause for optimism.
Meanwhile, long-term inflation expectations continue falling which might be troubling if they continue to do so. Fortunately, that's not likely without significant economic slowing that we'll see show up in the data long before any recession begins.
For a final look at recession risk, I like to use the St. Louis Fed's smoothed-out recession risk indicator. This looks at the risk of a recession beginning in the current month (it's actually delayed two months). It uses a four-month running average of leading economic indicators.
(Source: St. Louis Federal Reserve )
Since 1967, this smoothed out recession probability estimator has predicted five of the last seven recessions before they have started. The key is that as long as the recession risk is at 3.9% or below, the economy is very unlikely to be in a recession. At 0.24% risk right now, this confirms that the US economy is likely to keep expanding for the foreseeable future.
Bottom Line: The Fed's Gift To The Market Might Not Actually Be As Large As We Think Again, I'm not a market timer, just a macroeconomics nerd (my major in college) who wants to ensure I and my readers see the big picture. Any estimates of when recessions and bear markets are likely to begin are purely based on historical averages, and the most time-tested models we have. They are probabilistic and not definition predictions that should be used for market timing purposes.
Basically, these weekly economic updates are not meant for market timing purposes, but rather to allow you to prepare yourself emotionally and financially for when a recession does inevitably happen. It's also meant to give you around a year's warning (hopefully longer) to adapt your portfolio's capital allocation strategy.
That might mean:
Stockpiling some cash (to take advantage of future bargains during a bear market); Putting new capital to work in more defensive companies (utilities, healthcare, telecom, consumer staples); or For the most risk-averse investors, potentially moving some money into bonds or cash equivalents (asset allocation changes). Personally, I used the recent correction to take advantage of incredible bargains. That means loading up on 11 quality, undervalued blue-chip companies. In fact, I recently added Apple ( AAPL ) and Brookfield Property Partners ( BPY ) to that list as well (and bought BPY last week). That's because the actual macroeconomic and corporate fundamentals do not indicate this is the start of a bear market. In fact, based on the best models and current data we have (that factor in nearly two dozen leading indicators), the next bear market and recession are likely to start:
recession: around late 2020 to mid-2021 (most likely early 2021 at the earliest) bear market: around mid-2020 to late 2020 at the earliest I'm not being especially defensive since I'm still 100% in stocks and have no plans to sell before the next market downturn starts. Nor do I recommend most investors switch from their current long-term investment plans, which should already have you in the right asset allocation that best meets your personal needs and risk profile.
Rest assured that if the macro trends (both economic and earnings) shift and point to a recession (and bear market) coming within the next 12 to 18 months, you'll read about it here. But for now, investors can cheer that the more dovish Fed they've been hoping for appears to have finally arrived.
Of course, that also means that we're likely to see slower growth and lower inflation, which is what will allow the Fed to potentially stop after just two more rate hikes. While Wall Street loves the idea of getting back to the "new normal" of slower growth and lower rates of the past decade, investors will want to watch the job market closely for signs of slowing job creation.
The simple fact is that when Main Street prospers so too does Wall Street. Thus, good growth is always superior over the long-term to anemic growth rates, even if it does allow for historically low interest rates and theoretically higher stock valuations. And we can't forget that the Fed's balance sheet roll-off remains in effect and potentially could be boosting the effective fed funds rate to levels far above the official metric. Which is why I'll continue to carefully monitor the economic fundamentals closely, for signs that the Fed is still overtightening and possibly making another policy mistake.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL, BPY.
